nameStory: The name 'flavidus' comes from Latin meaning 'yellowish' or 'golden,' referring to this spider's distinctive pale coloration. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, spider enthusiasts sometimes call it the 'golden cobweb weaver' for its light-colored body and web-building habits.
description: Spintharus flavidus is a small cobweb spider that builds the classic tangled, sticky webs we often see in corners and crevices. This tiny arachnid has a yellowish to pale brown body with a rounded abdomen typical of comb-footed spiders. Like other members of its family, it's quite small, usually measuring just a few millimeters in body length. It belongs to a widespread group of spiders found from North America all the way down to South America.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Round, bulbous abdomen that feels soft and delicate if gently touched, with relatively thin legs compared to the body size

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Yellowish to pale golden-brown coloration overall, often with a slightly translucent appearance that makes internal structures faintly visible

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates messy, three-dimensional cobwebs that feel sticky to the touch and lack the organized pattern of orb weaver webs

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, with the body typically smaller than a peppercorn and easily overlooked without close inspection

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside down in its web and drops quickly when disturbed, often playing dead by curling up into a tight ball

habitat: Look for this spider in protected spots like under roof eaves, in woodsheds, basements, and other sheltered areas around human structures. It prefers areas with some moisture but not direct rain, often building webs in the corners where walls meet or in gaps between stored items. In natural settings, you might find it under rock overhangs or in hollow tree spaces.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build new webs in sheltered locations. This is when you're most likely to spot freshly constructed, clean-looking cobwebs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when spiders are most visible in their webs. Mating occurs during warm months, and females may be seen guarding small, papery egg sacs.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues but begins to slow as temperatures drop. Young spiders may disperse to find overwintering sites, sometimes appearing in new locations.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, but some may survive in very protected, warmer microclimates like heated basements. Egg sacs overwinter to produce next year's generation.

funFact: Despite being tiny enough to fit on your fingernail, this spider is part of an incredibly successful family that has colonized two entire continents, with the same species found in backyards from New England all the way to the rainforests of Bolivia!
confusionNotes: This spider can be easily confused with other small cobweb spiders, especially common house spiders. The key difference is the distinctly yellowish coloration - most house spiders are darker brown or gray. Remember: 'Yellow fellow in the cobweb' for Spintharus flavidus.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'cobweb' comes from the old English word 'coppe,' meaning spider, so cobweb literally means 'spider web.' These webs were once commonly seen covered in dew or dust in corners of old buildings, giving rise to the phrase 'clearing out the cobwebs.'
compareHints: Since this is the only Spintharus species documented in New England, compare it with other small Theridiidae family members like house spiders and widow spiders. Unlike the dark, robust common house spider, S. flavidus is much more delicate and distinctly pale yellow. Unlike widow spiders, it completely lacks the glossy black coloration and distinctive markings, appearing almost translucent by comparison.
